t: Hello, and welcome.
In this audio program we walk you through Meaning Intelligence — the cognitive operating system of the meaning civilization.
By the end, you will have a clear picture of the book's core question, its version-seven upgrade, and why this theory had to emerge now.

Chapter One begins with the most fundamental change in this edition: the book has evolved from a "theoretical ecosystem" into a complete "evidence architecture." Every theoretical proposition has been converted into a testable hypothesis.
Every core concept now carries an explicit evidence grade.
The original equations have been upgraded into dynamically estimable models, and all related experiments are pre-registered.
Evidence is graded from E-zero to E-six: E-zero means a concept has only been defined; E-six means it has survived external validation across contexts and cultures.
And the book's academic integrity pledge centers on one word: falsifiability.
If any core module reaches its failure threshold in a pre-registered experiment, the corresponding chapter will be flagged or removed in later editions.
So why does this theory need to exist at all?

Look around the intelligence era and you will see a striking rupture: logical, computational, and perceptual intelligences are advancing rapidly, yet the capacity to judge whether something is worth doing has never been systematically theorized or engineered.
AI can answer "how to do it," but more and more people are asking "what is it for?" The book's core diagnosis is this: power and meaning are separating.
Capability cares only about reaching goals faster and more accurately; meaning asks whether the goal itself is worthwhile.
No existing theory of intelligence has built directional judgment into its own definition — and that theoretical vacuum is exactly what Meaning Intelligence fills.
Crucially, Meaning Intelligence is not a new intelligence sitting beside IQ or EQ.
It is a meta-intelligence: a capacity that regulates the direction of all other intelligent activities.
Other intelligences answer "can we do it?" Meaning Intelligence answers "is it worth doing, worth it for whom, and at what scale?" Why now?
Because three turning points have converged.
The technological turning point: general AI and bioengineering keep expanding what we can do, making the choice of direction urgent.
The social turning point: a deepening crisis of trust has loosened the old meaning systems.
The cognitive turning point: information overload makes people hunger for clear anchors of meaning.

The entire argument rests on three scientific battle lines: the science of civilizational risk — can instability be quantified; the science of cognitive leaps — can they be observed and trained; and Meaning-AI engineering — can it improve long-term decision quality.
The pledge applies to all three: if any line fails its pre-registered experiments, the corresponding modules are marked falsified.
No forcing the argument.
In short, Chapter One explains why we need Meaning Intelligence now: the rupture between "can do" and "worth doing," and the urgency of closing it.
Chapter Two builds the core theoretical system.
A rigorous theory needs foundations, so we begin with four axioms — the indivisible assumptions from which everything else grows.
Axiom one: meaning arises from the tension between finitude and openness.
Our time, resources, and cognition are limited, so we must choose — and choosing generates meaning.
Yet the future is open and uncertain, so we need direction.
An eternal, infinite being would need neither choices nor direction — and therefore no Meaning Intelligence.
Axiom two: meaning must be perceivable by a subject, yet does not depend on subjective feelings.
There is a difference between "this thing is meaningful" and "I feel it is meaningful." The integrity of an ecosystem is meaningful to future generations even if no one alive feels it now.
Meaning is an objective worthiness-relation between a subject and a larger system.
Axiom three: meanings at different scales cannot be reduced to one another, but they can be coordinated.
Personal, organizational, national, and civilizational meanings cannot simply be added up.
But they can be dynamically prioritized and phased.
Developing the economy and protecting the environment serve different scales — neither simply outranks the other; they are coordinated across stages.
Axiom four: every meaning judgment is inherently incomplete.
We always judge with partial information under time pressure — a reasonable approximation, never a perfect, once-and-for-all conclusion.
Meaning Intelligence is a process, not a verdict; it must keep iterating.
These four axioms specify no concrete content, only formal conditions — they are the constitution of Meaning Intelligence.
Now the core definition: Meaning Intelligence is a meta-intelligence — the capacity to regulate the direction of all other intelligent activities.
It never asks "can it be done?" It asks "is it worth doing, for whom, and at what scale?" Meaning itself has a clear structure.

Vertically, it spans a continuous spectrum: at the top, the meta-meaning level — ultimate directions such as life's continuation, freedom, creation, symbiosis; in the middle, the intermediary level — institutions, culture, language, evaluative systems that carry meaning; at the bottom, the situational level — immediate judgments in concrete scenes.
These are not three separated boxes but one spectral band, from abstract and long-cycle at the top to concrete and short-cycle at the bottom.

Horizontally, every complete meaning judgment has three dimensions: direction — where are we going, forward or backward, expanding or converging; value — which value is served: utility, intrinsic, or relational; and boundary — where do we stop, in time, space, or relationship.
Missing any one, the judgment is incomplete.
The dynamic structure is meaning potential: the value-distance between the current state and the ideal direction.
High potential drives us to act and change; low potential feels like stability and ease — and it updates continuously with new data.
Meaning structures do fail, most often through conflicts between levels or dimensions: individual freedom versus organizational discipline; utility gained while relationships are damaged.
Where the essence is shared, differences can coexist harmoniously.
This brings us to the five-scale navigation model: individual, organization, city, nation, humanity.

Each scale has its own irreducible meaning logic — individuals live by narrative and a sense of existence; organizations by mission legitimacy and a reason to persist; cities by place and collective memory; nations by shared destiny and institutional meaning; humanity by civilizational direction and species responsibility.
You cannot say a nation's meaning is the sum of personal meanings — the logics differ entirely.
Yet meanings transmit between scales: upward, personal meanings resonate and emerge into civilizational meaning; downward, civilizational direction quietly shapes individual choices.
When scales align, resonance amplifies meaning; when they conflict, we return to the meta-meaning level and recalibrate recursively — never a simple weighted average.
How does this relate to existing theories?
Meaning Intelligence replaces nothing; it fills a shared blind spot: no existing theory has systematized, structured, and engineered directional judgment.
Existentialism names the absurd but offers no operational tools.
Ethics covers normative judgment, but meaning judgment includes far more than morality — the good is only one input.
Positive psychology measures subjective well-being; Meaning Intelligence tracks objective meaning potential.
AI-alignment research injects values; Meaning Intelligence gives AI an architecture for generating meaning.

Finally, eighteen core propositions have all been converted into testable hypothesis cards, each with operational definitions, measurable variables, pre-registered falsification criteria, and current evidence grades.
Hypothesis one — that Meaning Intelligence is a necessary meta-layer — would be falsified if systems without an MI module showed no higher drift in long-term decision direction than systems with one.
Testable, falsifiable, fallible: that is the book's integrity.
Chapter Three turns theory into a working, deployable system.
The overall framework is the MI Engine under spectral-spiral binding.

The old three fixed levels become a continuous spectral band — from abstract to concrete with no gaps — and the underlying mechanism is the spiral with binding: each judgment loops back and slightly recalibrates the deeper cognition, sharpening direction without hardening into rigidity.

The familiar three modules — perception, judgment, action — and four processes — identification, evaluation, decision, revision — are not separate parts; they are projections of one spiral cycle at different phases.
Perception extracts meaning-relevant signals from the environment and internal states, encodes them, and outputs a list of meaning events.
Judgment computes meaning potential for the current state, evaluates the options, and outputs a directional recommendation.
Action converts that recommendation into executable decisions, with action directives and monitoring metrics.
The four processes are the spiral's four checkpoints each revolution.
Meaning identification, triggered by new signals or scheduled inspection, collects and ranks signals into a briefing.
Meaning evaluation quantifies impact, computes current potential, and surfaces conflicts and opportunities in a situation report.
Meaning decision filters options and coordinates multi-scale conflicts into a ranked choice.
Meaning feedback and revision, after action, compares results with expectations, analyzes deviation, and sends corrections back.
The revision mechanism is layered.
Deviation under ten percent triggers a level-one correction — fine-tuning execution, effective immediately.
Ten to thirty percent triggers a level-two correction — adjusting mid-level indicator systems on weekly or monthly cycles.
Above thirty percent, or any system-level conflict, triggers a level-three correction — recalibrating the deepest meta-meaning direction on yearly, even generational, cycles.

Feedback itself flows in four kinds — same-level, cross-level, cross-module, and cross-scale — and the system learns: every complete cycle is archived in a case library, effective direction patterns are distilled into rules, and a diversity reward guards against overfitting, so the engine keeps optimizing itself without external maintenance.
The three signature properties distinguish MI from every other intelligence.
Meta-cognitive awareness is its eyes: while judging meaning, it can examine its own judging framework.
Spiral ascent is its path: every cycle goes a little deeper, never repeating, never spinning in place.
Active zeroing is its courage: when the current meaning structure has failed, it deliberately resets key parts — before collapse forces the issue.

On the engineering side, the MI Engine has four layers: a data layer — time-series databases of meaning events, graph databases of meaning structures, vector databases of cases; an algorithm layer — potential computation, multi-scale arbitration, direction prediction; an interface layer — input, output, and human interaction, with every judgment explainable; and an application layer — scenarios for each of the five scales, wrapped in security and ethics by design: preventing adversarial inputs from distorting the meta-meaning constraints, making every critical decision traceable, and reserving a human final veto on key choices.

Deployment proceeds in four stages: a personal MI assistant as app or web tool; an organizational decision-support system; a city or regional governance dashboard; and finally a national, even civilizational, strategic simulation platform.
Chapter Four takes the theory into the real world, across five scales and six domains.
The upward transmission: personal meanings resonate and emerge into civilizational meaning — never a simple sum.
The downward transmission: civilizational direction guides individual choices — never a command.

When scales align, meaning resonates and is amplified; when they diverge — individual freedom against national security, urban growth against ecological boundaries — the answer is recursive recalibration from the meta-meaning level, not weighted averaging.
And a testable core hypothesis: if two scales' meaning directions diverge for long enough, at least one scale will enter a meaning crisis.
Now the six domains.
In education, spiral curriculum design: core concepts are never finished in one pass — each loop deepens the meaning, replacing rote memorization with deepening understanding.
In AI, alignment is not a one-time injection of values but a continuous spiral of conflict, dialogue, and revision, gradually aligning human and machine meaning-directions.
In medicine, end-of-life meaning zeroing: not abandoning care, but consciously shifting the meaning-direction from cure toward peace — so patients can close life with dignity.
In public policy, a meaning evaluation beside outcome evaluation: periodically asking whether this policy is still worth doing today, rather than clinging to old programs.
In art and media, the natural meaning-zeroing devices: by breaking old frames of perception, they open space for new meaning to emerge.

Across scales, the tools differ: for individuals, life-narrative mapping and personal zeroing protocols for moments of meaning rigidity; for organizations, mission stress-testing and full organizational zeroing procedures; for cities, meaning monitoring models guarding place and collective memory against placeless sameness; for nations, institutions — constitutions, laws, education — carrying shared destiny, with post-war Germany's meaning reconstruction as a spiral case; and for humanity, a whole-civilization diagnosis of the widening gap between cognitive advance and behavioral lag — a decoupling crisis at the meaning level.
Chapter Five zooms out to civilizational evolution.

The pivotal claim: civilization itself is a meaning-intelligence system running at a super-large scale and super-long cycle — a giant meaning engine continuously adjusting direction across the four spectral dimensions of cognition, value, existence, and action.
Read through this framework, civilization's history obeys four laws.
The law of synchronous evolution: the four dimensions must evolve in step for the system to stay healthy.
The law of decoupling crisis: when any dimension runs far ahead or falls behind, decoupling appears — and that is a meaning crisis.
The law of spiral depth: the depth of meaning gained from each civilizational cycle is proportional to the thoroughness of active zeroing.
The law of binding resilience: how long a civilization endures is directly tied to its capacity to keep the four dimensions bound.
The great transitions — the Axial Age, the Enlightenment, today's ecological turn — all fit this pattern.

At civilizational scale, Meaning Intelligence has four jobs: continuously monitoring the binding state of the four dimensions; providing early warning of decoupling risks; supplying professional counsel when zeroing is due; and navigating civilization's long-term direction.
The long-term roadmap has five stages.
From now to 2030: cognitive popularization and tool incubation — this book plus personal tools.
2030 to 2045: organizational application and institutional embedding — organizational standards, integration into education.
2045 to 2060: city and regional meaning governance — urban meaning monitoring systems.
2060 to 2080: national and civilizational architecture — national systems and civilizational monitoring.
And after 2080: human-level Meaning Intelligence and civilizational self-awareness — active zeroing and spiral governance at the scale of the species.

The book's four core contributions: defining Meaning Intelligence as the necessary meta-layer of intelligence, filling the rupture between "can do" and "worth doing"; establishing the spectral-spiral binding theory; articulating the three signature properties — meta-cognitive awareness, spiral ascent, active zeroing; and delivering a complete verification path from five scales to six domains, with executable tools.

And the boundaries are stated honestly: it applies only to systems with subjects; it cannot replace professional expertise — not a doctor's diagnosis, not an engineer's design; it promises no unique right answer, only a more worthwhile direction; and excessive meta-cognition can paralyze decision-making.
The appendices are the book's toolbox — for practitioners and researchers alike, four parts.

First, the practice toolkit: for individuals — a daily meaning dictionary card, an annual personal meaning zeroing protocol, and a life-narrative spiral map for long-term tracking; for organizations — a mission meta-cognitive stress test, a strategic organizational zeroing protocol, and a quarterly meaning dashboard; for cities — a citizen meaning census and community zeroing workshops; plus universal tools — a spiral-state tracking table and a zeroing safety checklist to run before every reset.

Second, core variables and scales: precise definitions and value ranges for meaning potential, direction consistency, binding strength and more; established instruments such as the Personal Meaning Clarity Scale and the four-dimensional spectral self-assessment; and the Witness dual-channel measurement — channel A self-report, channel B behavioral tasks — integrated into one composite score.

Third, the meta-intelligence six-layer application framework: from lightening load at layer one to reflective recursive review at layer six, each layer specifying its core question, method, evidence grade, and common pitfalls — three closed loops stacked, with typical forms for each of the five scales — and the stack itself flagged as a testable structure with its own evidence grade.

Fourth, the falsification matrix and index: all eighteen hypotheses with their falsification conditions and evidence grades, a theory-failure matrix stating what happens if each module fails, and quick indexes of terms and tools.
The whole apparatus exists so the theory lands in your hands: whether you want to clarify your own direction or run serious research, the support materials are ready to use.
Let us close with the whole book in view.

Philosophically, it answers whether meaning is subjective or objective: meaning is the cognition and judgment of the worthiness-relation between one's own actions and a larger system — not a mere feeling.
Theoretically and mechanically, it delivers the spectral-spiral binding theory and a complete operating framework: three levels, three modules, four processes, and the three signature properties.

In practice and engineering, it provides five-scale programs, six domain cases, and a full engineering interface from data layer to application layer — proof that Meaning Intelligence can actually be deployed.
And it is candid about limits: subject-systems only; no replacement for expertise; no unique answers; and a warning against meta-cognitive paralysis.

At civilizational scale, it reframes civilization as a macro meaning-intelligence system governed by the four laws, and lays out the five-stage roadmap toward human-level meaning intelligence and civilizational self-awareness.

The book ends with words worth remembering: the ultimate purpose of Meaning Intelligence is not to make humanity more successful, but to help humanity live more wide-awake — clearly knowing what we are doing, why we are doing it, within what boundaries, and when to stop and ask again what is truly worthwhile.
Its aim is to move humanity from a passive entity swept along by history to a self-aware subject of evolution — the very mark of a mature civilization.
So here is the closing question, for you: does your current direction in life match your own worthiness judgment?
If it has drifted — do you have the courage to run a meaning zeroing on yourself?
Thank you for listening.
